### 13.3 Build primitives: `resolve` and the face-list accessors
- V1 The `input_passthrough` sketch (§8.8) calls two of the primitives below without defining them. [§8.8]
- V2 All three are normative in the forms given here (D-061). [D-061] (bold)
- V3 This section gives the three forms, the two duties resolution enforces, which client each duty binds and why, and the standing of `resolve_terminal`.
- V4 `resolve(assembly, path::String) → AbstractComponent` resolves an immediate child, a container element's key segment included.
- V5 `input_faces(c)` / `output_faces(c) → Vector{String}` return the stringified keys of a leaf's `u_types` / `y_types` (the key set is `T`-independent).
- V6 For an assembly they return the entries of `input_wires(c)` / `output_wires(c)`.
- V7 Declaration order is preserved, which gives deterministic printouts and stable diagnostics.
- V8 `resolve_terminal(assembly, path) → (component, name)` splits off a terminal path's final segment and resolves the prefix through `resolve`.
- V9 The split is unambiguous because face names (the names ports wear on their component's boundary) may contain dots but never slashes (§8.6). [§8.6]
- V10 Resolution enforces two duties, and they belong to different clients.
- V11 The first is the one-level rule (§6.1, D-207). [§6.1, D-207]
- V12 A connection endpoint resolves to an immediate child and one of its faces.
- V13 A wiring path reaching further is a build error, `PathResolution`, whatever the declared field types along it.
- V14 The second is the generic-holding rule, which governs the deep paths the read side still writes.
- V15 It is enforced by the service walk, which follows declared field types alongside instances.
- V16 A segment that traverses past a generically-held field (one whose declared type is non-concrete) is a diagnostic, even though the concrete instance in hand would resolve it.
- V17 Resolving to a generic child is port-level access and legal.
- V18 An unknown segment errors with the sibling field list in hand.
- V19 Paths are validated before anything runs on them, and renames break loudly (D-061, D-130). [D-061, D-130]
- V20 Which rule applies depends on who is resolving (D-130). [D-130] (bold)
- V21 D-083 separates the reads a build's correctness rests on from the reads that only observe it. [D-083]
- V22 The same line runs through resolution.
- V23 Three kinds of client share one resolution, and each gets the rule its promises require.
- V24 wiring
- V25 connection declarations, in the structure step
- V26 the one-level rule: an immediate child and one of its faces
- V27 service
- V28 condition entries (the path-addressed sparse overlay that sets a build's state), trim `reads`, taps, device read bindings (§14.3, §14.7, §14.10, §11.2, D-406) [§14.3, §14.7, §14.10, §11.2, D-406]
- V29 strict: no traversal past a generic child, checked at the authoring or mount level
- V30 inspection
- V31 snapshot and log inspection (D-310) [D-310]
- V32 the instance walk
- V33 Each client's treatment has its own warrant.
- V34 Wiring is what the law (§6.1) is stated for, so wiring resolution applies that law verbatim. [§6.1]
- V35 Under one-level routing the generic-holding question never arises there, because an endpoint stops before any field it could traverse past.
- V36 Service paths are checked at the authoring or mount level for two reasons.
- V37 First, the locality law is an authoring-level law, and absolute paths are a compiled derivative (§14.2). [§14.2]
- V38 Second, the mount itself checks a mount prefix, where the problem's authored names resolve through the export chain from the mount point (§14.9). [§14.9]
- V39 So the service check covers the authored path below that prefix.
- V40 Drift stays loud.
- V41 A binding's unknown path or name is refused at attach, as a `PathResolution` or a `ReadResolution`, with a did-you-mean (the offending name plus the list-in-hand it should have matched) (D-406). [D-406]
- V42 Inspection walks instances instead.
- V43 A generic seam is not an error for a client that never claimed substitutability.
- V44 "What is in this build" is inspection's defining question.
- V45 The scoping is one principle, not three concessions.
- V46 What varies across the three clients is not how far a client is trusted.
- V47 It is what a violation costs, and where the cost lands.
- V48 An inspection client claims no substitutability.
- V49 It addresses one build's instances, and a broken inspection read fails at its own site, harming only the observer.
- V50 A wiring entry is carried by the declaring type and compiled into every instantiation.
- V51 That is why its endpoints stop at the boundary.
- V52 A wire reaching past one would fail at substitution time, at a different site, for whoever exercised the substitution the field advertised.
- V53 That is the non-local failure class the error discipline exists to eliminate (§8.4). [§8.4]
- V54 The rule is strict exactly where a promise depends on it, and relaxed exactly where none is made (D-083, D-130). [D-083, D-130]
- V55 Strictness forbids nothing outright for a service path.
- V56 Declaring the field's concrete type restores the deep read legally, with the hard-coding visible in the declaration itself.
- V57 For wiring there is no deep route left to restore, because the face chain is the route (§6.1). [§6.1]
- V58 Which of the three rules a client resolves under is internal framework fact, never user-facing API (D-130). [D-130]
- V59 The two ways of applying one plan (§14.4) use the same arrangement and have the same status. [§14.4]
- V60 Inside the framework only wiring resolution calls `resolve_terminal`.
- V61 The services and the readers split their own paths through the service walk (§14.3, §14.4). [§14.3, §14.4]

### 13.4 Runtime failures: one catch site, an execution cursor
- V62 A runtime failure is a throw inside a frame (one iteration of the loop) or inside boundary zero, the initialization boundary, which runs the ordinary macro-sequence with an empty integrate.
- V63 The framework catches it at one site, records where execution stood, and names how to reproduce it.
- V64 This section covers, in order, where a failure is caught, the runtime carrier, the interrupt, the disposition, reproduction, boundary zero, the nonfinite check and device-side failures.

#### Where a failure is caught
- V65 The `Model`'s `frame!` wraps each whole frame, every boundary it settles included, in a single `try`, and its `init!` wraps boundary zero the same way (D-317). [D-317] (bold)
- V66 The `Model` is the deployment and its executor at one scalar.
- V67 A boundary's macro-sequence runs integrate → project → event iteration → ticks → publication.
- V68 `frame!` never wraps per stage or per component (D-059). [D-059] (bold)
- V69 The loop wraps each frame in a `try` of its own, which decides the failure's disposition (below) and builds no carrier (D-317). [D-317]
- V70 Framing information does not need to be caught into existence.
- V71 The executor (the compiled form of the stage execution order) maintains an execution cursor, a plain mutable field of the executor recording where execution stands in the compiled order (D-059). [D-059]
- V72 The cursor records three facts.
- V73 The first is the component, by its index in the structure's component list, the index the execution order lists (D-261). [D-261]
- V74 That order is the one `Outputs` (the nominal evaluation's product, the port classes and the execution order) carries.
- V75 The second is which function is running, one of `y_state`, `y_direct`, `x_deriv`, `s_update`, a guard, a handler, or `x_projection`.
- V76 The third is the boundary phase, one of the frame-top drain, integration stage k, the arrival sweep (one pass through the execution order), the θ = 0 validation, a localization trial, projection, event round r, or the ticks.
- V77 Maintaining the cursor costs one cheap store per dispatch on a single-tasked executor, with no allocation and no exception handlers.
- V78 It covers every user-code surface uniformly, including the forgettable ones.
- V79 Those are the RHS evaluations at interior RK stage points and the guard evaluations at the trial points of ITP or Brent root-finding (§10.4). [§10.4]
- V80 [code block] # the cursor: one mutable field of the executor, overwritten per dispatch

#### The runtime carrier
- V81 The catch site wraps the original exception in `StepError`, the runtime counterpart of the `DiagnosticError` carrier (the single exception diagnostics travel in when thrown).
- V82 A `StepError` carries five things.
- V83 They are the cursor frame (the copy of the cursor a `StepError` carries), the time, the frame-entry boundary index, the host of the catch, and the original exception as `cause`.
- V84 The time is the clock at the failure, a boundary time in a boundary phase, the stage or trial time inside integration.
- V85 The frame-entry boundary index is the replay pointer (D-128). [D-128] (bold)
- V86 It names the frame-top boundary at which the failing frame began.
- V87 That frame top is a grid boundary or boundary zero, and it is always a legal replay halt (§12.7). [§12.7]
- V88 The host names the catch that took the throw.
- V89 It is `:loop` for a throw inside a frame, and `:boundary_zero` for a throw inside the boundary zero that `init!` runs.
- V90 A `StepError` renders under the doctrine of §13.2. [§13.2]
- V91 The cursor frame and the reproduction come first, the cause second, and names are strings.
- V92 Conformance failure (§9.5) needs no separate path. [§9.5]
- V93 At the table-write point it throws as every fail-fast site does, a `DiagnosticError` holding the one diagnostic, and it arrives at the same catch site (D-235). [D-235]
- V94 The catch site unwraps a single-diagnostic `DiagnosticError` thrown inside the guarded sequence, and the `StepError`'s `cause` is that diagnostic (D-221). [D-221] (bold)
- V95 That unwrapping is the species rule.
- V96 A species of `StepError` is one whose `cause` is a diagnostic.
- V97 The conformance failure's species carries the field-diff payload (the structured data a diagnostic carries beside its kind).
- V98 The rule keeps the catch site the only `StepError` constructor.
- V99 A `StepError` arriving at the catch site is therefore an invariant failure, while a runtime check stays a plain thrower of its kind (D-221). [D-221]
- V100 A collected carrier has no single kind and rides as `cause` unchanged.
- V101 No runtime check throws one.
- V102 The cause's type is the carrier's parameter (D-225). [D-225] (bold)
- V103 `StepError{C}` takes the type of its `cause`, bounded to a diagnostic or an exception.
- V104 A species is therefore `StepError{Kind}`, and a raw throw is `StepError{ArgumentError}` and the like.
- V105 `isa StepError` matches both (D-225). [D-225]
- V106 A test asserts a species as `@test_throws StepError{ConformanceFailure}`, the runtime spelling of the build carrier's idiom (§13.2). [§13.2]
- V107 A collected carrier riding as `cause` is an exception and falls under that arm.
- V108 A bare value thrown deliberately by model code is neither, and the constructor refuses it unframed.
- V109 The framework does not handle that throw (D-225). [D-225]
- V110 The cursor frame and the pointer are then lost, and the lifecycle does not move as it does on the framed path.
- V111 [code block] # the runtime carrier: its parameter the cause's type — a diagnostic's kind

#### The interrupt
- V112 An `InterruptException` is the one exception the catch site never wraps (D-317). [D-317]
- V113 It is not model code failing.
- V114 It is the operator's stop command (§12.4). [§12.4]
- V115 So the catch site discriminates it and routes it to the stop path (D-132). [D-132]
- V116 The run takes the ordinary graceful tail and ends `stopped`, never `errored` under a `StepError`.
- V117 With the boundary masking in force (§12.4) a single interrupt never reaches the branch. [§12.4]
- V118 It is deferred to a frame-top, wait or pause-block unmask point (§12.4, D-294), and never raises inside the guarded sequence. [§12.4, D-294]
- V119 Julia's forced throw after repeated interrupts does reach it, with the disposition §12.4 gives it (D-398). [§12.4, D-398]
- V120 The branch is kept for that case and defensively, because the cost of being wrong about the masking is a terminally errored session in place of a clean stop.

#### The disposition
- V121 The `Simulation` ends in a terminal status, `stopped` or `errored`, with the exception retrievable (D-059). [D-059]
- V122 A synchronous unattended run (a run with empty staging and no snapshot readers) rethrows after the shutdown tail completes, so CI fails honestly.
- V123 An interactive session logs the rendered error.
- V124 `run!` and `replay!` discriminate the two by the roster (D-268). [D-268] (bold)
- V125 With no device (any attached participant in the periphery) rostered the run is unattended and rethrows.
- V126 With one or more it logs the rendered error through the logging backend and returns, the lifecycle reading `errored` and `termination(sim)` retaining the cause.
- V127 `step!` is deviceless by construction (§12.6, D-389) and always rethrows. [§12.6, D-389]

#### Reproduction
- V128 Reproducibility holds by construction.
- V129 Staged inputs are drained and recorded to the trace (the primary record of a session) at the frame top, before the boundary executes.
- V130 So the failing boundary's inputs are already in the trace when it fails.
- V131 The error names the frame-entry boundary `k` to replay to.
- V132 `replay!(sim2, trc; to_boundary = k)` halts exactly at that frame top (D-128). [D-128]
- V133 It halts in `:replay`, the input mode that keeps the recording attached, so the failing frame's record is still ahead of the simulation (§12.7, D-218). [§12.7, D-218]
- V134 `step!` then applies that record and re-executes the failing frame under instrumentation, localized boundaries included.
- V135 [code block] replay!(sim2, trc; to_boundary = k)   # halt at the frame top; still :replay

#### Boundary zero
- V136 Boundary zero is caught too, under the service's disposition (D-223). [D-223] (bold)
- V137 Boundary zero runs inside `init!`, a stopped-sim service, not inside the loop.
- V138 The simulation's `init!` calls `init!` on its `Model`, which runs boundary zero.
- V139 Its macro-sequence executes the same user-code surfaces the frame's does, with the cursor maintained through them, so the `Model`'s `init!` hosts the same catch (D-317). [D-317]
- V140 A throw inside boundary zero arrives as a `StepError` from the one constructor.
- V141 Its cursor frame comes from the cursor, its time is `t₀`, and the species rule applies.
- V142 Any throw inside boundary zero writes the `Model`'s status back to `:built`, which returns the simulation's lifecycle to `built` (§12.6). [§12.6]
- V143 An `InterruptException` inside boundary zero is not model code failing, and it has no stop path to take in a service.
- V144 The host therefore lets it propagate raw, unwrapped.
- V145 The pointer is `0`.
- V146 A throw inside boundary zero leaves no trace and no checkpoint (the `Model`'s state at a frame top as one value).
- V147 The run `init!` opened stays behind, empty and with no trace header, and the run before it is gone.
- V148 Nothing can use it, since `trace(sim)` and the advances refuse a `built` simulation.
- V149 `init!` takes the trace header only after boundary zero publishes (§11.5). [§11.5]
- V150 The reproduction of a boundary-zero failure is `init!` under the same condition (D-274). [D-274] (bold)
- V151 Boundary zero is frame one's entry boundary too, so a frame-one failure carries the same pointer.
- V152 The carrier's `host` tells the two apart, and the rendered recipe reads it.
- V153 A frame-one failure has a trace, and the halt-then-`step!` recipe above holds for it at pointer `0`.
- V154 The halt restores the header and stops there, and `step!` re-executes frame one from the record.
- V155 Boundary zero's disposition differs from the loop's as well.
- V156 Nothing was published and no advance was under way, so there is no tail to take and no snapshot to promote.
- V157 The simulation returns to `built`.
- V158 `run!` and `step!` refuse it and name `init!` (§12.6), while `init!`, `restore!` and `replay!` remain legal. [§12.6]
- V159 The remedy for a condition that fails at `t₀` is a corrected condition, and `init!` re-establishes every store (the framework-owned home of one of a component's state letters) before it applies one (§14.1). [§14.1]
- V160 No termination record is written.
- V161 The stores may hold the half-transitioned `t₀` state until the next `init!`, `restore!` or `replay!` resets them.
- V162 They are retained for inspection, as an errored simulation's are (§13.6). [§13.6]
- V163 `trim!`'s commit is an `init!` (§14.8) and inherits the rule (D-223). [§14.8, D-223]

#### The nonfinite check
- V164 Divergence is not termination.
- V165 Dynamics that blow up (ground penetration, an unstable gain) produce NaNs that defeat guards.
- V166 NaN comparisons are false, so no declared guard will catch them.
- V167 An `isfinite` pass over the flat state buffer, run by the model after every return from the integrator backend, fails fast as `NonfiniteState`, a `StepError` species naming the component, the state leaf and the frame-entry boundary.
- V168 It catches diverging models generally, not just post-terminal ones.
- V169 Placement is the whole value.
- V170 The pass is the boundary's first act (D-157). [D-157] (bold)
- V171 It runs immediately after integrate returns, before `x_projection` and before the boundary sweep.
- V172 Run there, `NonfiniteState` names the component whose own block diverged.
- V173 Run later, the NaN has already propagated.
- V174 It reaches an innocent downstream component through the ordinary signal path and surfaces as that component's lookup-table `DomainError`, or as an `InexactError` in its conversion.
- V175 That is the error-locality inversion (§8.4), designed out of the build and quietly reintroduced at runtime. [§8.4]
- V176 One `isfinite` pass over a flat buffer is cheap enough that placement, not cost, decides.
- V177 `ẋ` does not participate in the check (D-157). [D-157] (bold)
- V178 A nonfinite derivative contaminates its own state block's step result within that very step.
- V179 The `x` check at the next boundary is therefore the same detection with identical component attribution.
- V180 And `ẋ` buffers are integrator scratch.
- V181 They are written per stage, meaningful only inside a step, and not boundary-consistent in the sense the check is stated over.

#### Device-side failures
- V182 Under domain separation, device-side user code fails in the device's own domain, because loop bodies and mappings run on the device task (§11.4, §11.6). [§11.4, §11.6]
- V183 It fails in two classes (D-105). [D-105]
- V184 A genuine bug takes the per-device crash path.
- V185 The wrapper reports `DeviceCrash`, and the run goes on without the device unless its attachment set `should_abort` (the per-attachment failure policy, an `attach!` keyword) (§11.6). [§11.6]
- V186 The liveness heartbeat is how a hang shows instead (§12.2). [§12.2]
- V187 An unmappable datum is not a failure at all.
- V188 The loop body tolerates and reports it as `MalformedDatum` (§11.6). [§11.6]
- V189 Device code shares no mutable state with the model (D-022), so the two failure domains never mix. [D-022]

- V165a Blowing-up dynamics produce NaNs.

- V182a Device-side user code fails in the device's own domain.
